text.p: International Business Machines Corp's method of writing off substantial portions of the costs of software acquisitions conforms to standard industry practices, the company said in response to an article critical of the practice in Barron's December 23 issue.

"IBM's acounting for the Lotus acquisition was handled in full conformance with generally accepted accounting principles. We believe that our accounting actions associated with the Lotus acquisition were prudent," IBM said in a statement issued on Monday.

The Barron's article by Abraham Briloff, a professor of accounting and ethics at Binghamton Univerity, said IBM's earnings have been inflated by as much as 10 percent by aggressively writing-off "in process" research and development.

The article criticizes what it calls "obscure accounting rules" that have allowed companies to take a "big bath upfront," thereby boosting future earnings. Briloff used IBM's accounting for its Lotus acquisition as his central example.

But Robert Willens, Lehman Brothers' tax and accounting analyst, challenged how the article singled out IBM when Briloff's premise would require a change in generally accepted accounting practices (GAAP) that cover all high-technology companies.

"His problems are almost invariably with many elements of GAAP," the Lehman analyst said of Briloff's article. "IBM would be in violation of the accounting rules" if it did not conform to these practices, he added.
Briloff, a respected critic of corporate accounting practices, has a history of attacking certain well-known companies to make more general points, Willens said.
In this case, Willens believes Briloff has missed his mark: "The principle could be re-evaluted, but IBM is above reproach in my mind," Willens said.
In the Barron's article, Briloff computed that in the first nine months of 1996, IBM benefited to the tune of $401 million after-tax, or 10 percent of IBM's $3.84 billion in earnings.
The professor wrote that "a not-insignificant portion of the earnings to which IBM's fans now attach a growth multiple aren't economic profits at all, but mere accounting chimera."
Briloff could not be immediately reached for further comment.
In midafternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, IBM stock was off 1/2 at 154.
